text:
matt: Hey team, seeing a weird pattern in the Go client where long-running streaming responses + auth refreshes seem to exhaust the http/2 connection pool and cause dials to pile up. Not sure if it's a context propagation bug or transport config. Anyone seen this?

sara: Ugh, yes. We hit something similar in staging last week. Can you paste the Transport config and the snippet doing the auth refresh? :eyes: 

matt: Here's the simplified transport we use (we wrap it with a token refresher):
```go
tr := &http.Transport{
  Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment,
  DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 30 * time.Second, KeepAlive: 30 * time.Second}).DialContext,
  TLSHandshakeTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
  MaxIdleConns: 200,
  IdleConnTimeout: 90 * time.Second,
  MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 100,
  ForceAttemptHTTP2: true,
}
client := &http.Client{Transport: tr, Timeout: 0} // streaming responses
```
and the refresher does an http request using the same client when a 401 is seen.

jess: Two quick guesses: 1) if you do a blocking auth refresh on the same connection or one of the stream goroutines, it can hold the stream open; http2 multiplexing still needs streams, but servers can limit concurrent streams. 2) context cancellation not making it down to Transport.RoundTrip so idle conns stick around.

tyler: Also check if the token refresher sets its own context with no deadline. If lots of goroutines are created to refresh and they block on network, you'll run out of available streams and new dials will spin.

matt: Good points. The refresher uses a mutex+singleflight so we don't duplicate refreshes, but we call it synchronously from the request path when we see 401. Example: `token := refresh(ctx)` where refresh itself does `client.Do(reqWithRefresh)`. Maybe weird reentrancy.

sara: Reentrancy is risky. If refresh uses the same client Transport and the server enforces low MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, you can deadlock. Try making the refresh call use a separate short-lived http.Client with its own Transport that disables HTTP/2 multiplexing or has a bigger connection pool.

matt: Will try that. Any tuning suggestions for transport fields to avoid conn leaks?

jess: A few things we've had success with: set IdleConnTimeout to something reasonable (60s), tune MaxIdleConnsPerHost to match expected concurrency, and ensure you call resp.Body.Close() in all code paths. For streaming, avoid setting global client Timeout; pass per-request contexts.

tyler: Also consider setting Transport.DisableKeepAlives=false (default) but if you suspect stale connections, rotate the Transport periodically (new Transport every X minutes) to force fresh connections. Not ideal but effective under weird proxy behavior.

matt: Repro steps: spin up a server that accepts a stream, sleeps 2s per chunk, and a /refresh endpoint that also sleeps (to simulate slow KMS). Then fire 200 concurrent streaming requests that occasionally trigger auth refresh. I'll try separate transport for refresh first.

sara: If you need a quick patch, here's a pattern we've used for refresh calls:
```go
refreshTr := &http.Transport{DisableKeepAlives: false, MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 50, ForceAttemptHTTP2: false} // prevent multiplexing fights
refreshClient := &http.Client{Transport: refreshTr, Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
// use refreshClient for token refresh only
```
Switching ForceAttemptHTTP2 off is intentionally conservative: if the refresh path uses its own TCP connections it won't be competing for streams on the same HTTP/2 session.

matt: Nice. Quick question on context propagation: when a parent request context is cancelled, should we cancel the token-refresh context too? We currently pass the parent's ctx to refresh, which might cause the refresh to be cancelled mid-way.

jess: Prefer deriving a child context with a short deadline from the parent, e.g. `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, 15*time.Second)` and pass that to refresh. That avoids indefinite blocking but still respects parent cancellation.

tyler: Also instrument waiting goroutines: add a metrics counter for active refresh goroutines and open file/socket count. In past incidents we saw goroutine counts spike then fall slowly.

matt: Good checklist. I'll try: 1) refresh client with separate transport, 2) bounded refresh timeout, 3) ensure resp.Body.Close everywhere, 4) add metrics. Will report back with numbers.

deploy-bot: deploy queued: staging/token-refresh-experiment -> infra-staging (#1247) :rocket:

sara: LMK if you want me to pair when you run the load test. Happy to help trace with pprof and netstat.

matt: Thanks — will ping once I have a repro. For now marking this as a probable http2 stream exhaustion + reentrancy issue. :white_check_mark:
